newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Bad weather hampers Colombia troop pull-out.
newsitem.headline: Bad weather hampers Colombia troop pull-out.

text.p: Bad weather has hampered efforts to pull 5,000 troops out of Colombia's southern jungle so that 60 soldiers taken prisoner by leftist rebels almost nine months ago can be released, military sources said on Monday.

Gen. Agustin Ardila, commander of the Fourth Division, said heavy rain had grounded all helicopters. But he remained optimistic that the demilitarization of a 5,000 square mile (13,000 sq km) swathe of Caqueta province would be finished by the midnight deadline on Tuesday (0500 GMT Wednesday).

"There is heavy rain and I have not been able to move a single helicopter. If necessary I will move the helicopters by night and at the moment we are pulling troops out by land and river," Ardila told Reuters in a phone interview.
The demilitarization -- the first time the army has ceded such a large area to the country's leftist rebels -- was ordered by President Ernesto Samper two weeks ago.

The move was part of a deal to persuade Latin America's oldest and largest guerrilla group, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), to hand over the 60 soldiers it seized when it overran a military base in neighbouring Putumayo province on Aug. 30.

At least 27 soldiers died in the attack on the Las Delicias outpost, which marked the start of Latin America's longest-running hostage crisis -- largely overshadowed by the recent siege of the Japanese Embassy residence in Lima.

Once Colombian troops have left the zone, national and international observers will check that demilitarization was completed and the FARC will then have 15 days to free the soldiers, along with 10 marines captured in a separate battle in northwest Choco province in January.
If the handover goes according to plan, it would be one of the FARC's most significant politico-military victories in recent years.
Ardila warned, however, that his troops would not be confined to barracks outside the neutral zone but would continue regular counterinsurgency operations.
He also said he would be looking to sever what he claimed were rebel-managed cocaine smuggling routes out of the area.
